title: 1948 Arab–Israeli War
description: Second and final stage of the 1948 Palestine war
wiki_lead:
The 1948 Arab–Israeli War (15 May 1948 – 10 March 1949), also known as the First Arab–Israeli War, followed the civil war in Mandatory Palestine (29 November 1947 – 14 May 1948) as the second and final stage of the 1948 Palestine war. The civil war became a war of separate states with the Israeli Declaration of Independence on 14 May 1948, the end of the British Mandate for Palestine at midnight, and the entry of a military coalition of Arab states into the territory of Mandatory Palestine the following morning. The war formally ended with the 1949 Armistice Agreements which established the Green Line.
Since the 1917 Balfour Declaration and the 1920 creation of the British Mandate of Palestine, and in the context of Zionism and the mass migration of European Jews to Palestine, there had been tension and conflict between Arabs, Jews, and the British in Palestine. On 29 November 1947, the United Nations General Assembly voted in favor of the United Nations Partition Plan for Palestine, proposing to divide the territory into an Arab state, a Jewish state, and an internationally
administered corpus separatum for the cities of Jerusalem and Bethlehem. The land allocated to the
Arab State included about 43% of Mandatory Palestine. The land allocated to the Jewish State,
who constituted a third of the population, was 56% of Mandatory Palestine. While Jewish leaders
in Palestine supported the plan, leaders of the Palestinian Arab community and in the broader
Arab world did not. The following day, the conflict escalated into a civil war with attacks by Palestinian militias and mobs on Jewish areas. As the two communities battled, the British withdrew. 
In April 1948, Zionist forces launched an offensive codenamed Plan Dalet, during which they conquered and depopulated cities, villages, and territories in Mandatory Palestine in preparation for the establishment of a Jewish state. Just before the expiration of the British Mandate for Palestine, Zionist leaders announced the Israeli Declaration of Independence on 14 May 1948. The following morning, Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, and expeditionary forces from Iraq launched an invasion into Palestine, taking control of the Arab areas and attacking Israeli forces and settlements. The 10 months of fighting took place mostly on the territory of the British Mandate and in the Sinai Peninsula and southern Lebanon, interrupted by several truce periods.
By the end of the war, the State of Israel controlled about 78% of the former territory of Mandatory Palestine: all of the area that the UN had proposed for a Jewish state, as well as almost 60% of the area proposed for an Arab state, including Jaffa, Lydda and Ramla (Ramle) area, Upper Galilee, some parts of the Negev, the west coast as far as Gaza City, and a wide strip along the Tel Aviv–Jerusalem road. Israel also took control of West Jerusalem, which was meant to be part of an international zone for Jerusalem and its environs. Transjordan took control of East Jerusalem and what became known as the West Bank, annexing it the following year. The territory known today as the Gaza Strip was occupied by Egypt.
Expulsions of Palestinians, which had begun during the civil war, continued during the Arab-Israeli war. Hundreds of Palestinians were killed in multiple massacres, such as occurred in the expulsions from Lydda and Ramla. These events are known today as the Nakba (Arabic for "the catastrophe") and were the beginning of the Palestinian refugee problem. A similar number of Jews migrated, fled, or were expelled from Arab states in the three years following the war, 260,000 of whom went to Israel.

'War of Independence' in Israel) was the first large-scale military confrontation between the newly independent State of Israel and a coalition of Arab statesâprincipally Egypt, Transjordan (later Jordan), Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon âtriggered by the Arab rejection of United Nations General Assembly Resolution 181, which proposed partitioning the former British Mandate of Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states, and culminating in an Arab invasion immediately following Israel's declaration of independence on May 14, 1948. The war's interstate phase followed a preceding civil conflict within Palestine that erupted on November 30, 1947âthe day after the UN Partition voteâwhen Arab irregulars ambushed Jewish buses near Lod (Lydda) and attacked Jewish neighborhoods in Jerusalem and Haifa, during which Arab irregular forces and militias sought to prevent the partition's implementation through violence, leading to the collapse of Palestinian Arab society and the flight of over 300,000 Arabs before the formal invasion. Arab leaders, including those from the Arab League, explicitly aimed to thwart the emergence of a Jewish state, with statements such as Arab Higher Committee spokesman Jamal al-Husseini's assertion that Arabs would fight "with the last drop of our blood" to prevent partition, reflecting a commitment to resolve the conflict through force rather than negotiation. The invading armies, totaling around 25,000â30,000 troops initially against Israel's roughly 30,000, advanced on multiple fronts but suffered from poor coordination, inexperienced leadership, and internal rivalries, while Israeli forces, organized under the Haganah and later the Israel Defense Forces, leveraged superior motivation, internal lines of communication, and tactical adaptability to repel the assaults despite an international arms embargo. Key battles, such as the defense of Jerusalem and operations in the Negev, saw Israeli counteroffensives expand control beyond the UN-proposed borders, securing approximately 78 percent of Mandatory Palestine by the war's end in early 1949. The conflict resulted in armistice agreements between Israel and its adversaries from February to July 1949, establishing temporary "Green Line" borders that allocated the Gaza Strip to Egyptian control and the West Bank (including East Jerusalem) to Jordanian annexation, while leaving Palestinian statehood unrealized due to the Arab states' absorption of the designated territories. Casualties numbered about 6,000 Israelis (1 percent of the Jewish population) and 10,000â15,000 Arabs, including combatants and civilians, amid documented atrocities on both sides, though Israeli military successes enabled localized expulsions and prevented returns that contributed to the displacement of roughly 700,000 Palestinians. The refugee exodus stemmed from a combination of factors, including Arab leadership directives to evacuate strategic areasâsuch as Arab broadcasters telling Arabs within the Jewish state to temporarily evacuate ahead of invading armiesâwidespread panic from combat and rumors, and direct Israeli orders in certain villages to clear military zones, rather than a singular premeditated policy of ethnic cleansing, as evidenced by archival records showing Jewish efforts in some cases to halt flights. This war not only affirmed Israel's survival against existential threats but also entrenched regional divisions, with Arab defeat fostering narratives of catastrophe (Nakba) among Palestinians and narratives of miraculous independence among Israelis, setting the stage for enduring hostilities.
